meta.title: Day 8 Exam: Abstract Algebra I — Model Paper 4
meta.subject: Abstract Algebra I

glossary.definition: A group is a set with an associative binary operation, an identity element, and an inverse for every element. The operation combines any two elements into another element of the set.
A subgroup is a subset of a group that itself forms a group under the same operation. It contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses.
The left coset aH is the set of all products ah with h in H: one translate of the subgroup by multiplying every element on the left by a.
The right coset Ha is the set of all products ha with h in H: the translate obtained by multiplying every subgroup element on the right by a.
The index of H in G is the number of distinct left cosets of H in G. It can be finite even when both groups are infinite.
An equivalence relation groups elements into classes by a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
A partition is a collection of nonempty disjoint subsets whose union is the whole set. Each element belongs to exactly one part.
A bijection is a function that is both one-to-one and onto: every output has exactly one preimage. It shows that two sets have the same cardinality.
A cyclic group is a group whose every element is an integer power of one generator, or an integer multiple of one generator in additive notation.

The order of an element is the least positive integer power that gives the identity, if one exists; otherwise its order is infinite. This differs from the order of a group, which is its number of elements.
Lagrange’s theorem says that the order of a subgroup of a finite group divides the group order. The proof counts equally sized cosets in a partition.
An abelian group is a group in which every two elements commute: their product is independent of their order.
An isomorphism is a bijection between groups that preserves their operation. It identifies the same group structure with different labels.
A permutation is a bijection of a set to itself. Permutations form a group under composition.
A cycle is a permutation that sends each listed element to the next and the last back to the first, fixing elements not listed. Disjoint cycles move disjoint sets of elements.
The alternating group A_n is the subgroup of S_n consisting of even permutations, those expressible as an even number of transpositions.
The dihedral group D₄ is the group of eight symmetries of a square: four rotations and four reflections, composed as transformations.
A coset representative is one chosen group element used to name a coset. Different elements of the same coset name the same subset.
A unit modulo n is a residue class that has a multiplicative inverse modulo n, equivalently a class represented by an integer relatively prime to n.
Euler’s totient φ(n) counts the residue classes modulo n that are relatively prime to n, equivalently the number of units modulo n.
A proper subgroup is a subgroup different from the whole group. The identity-only subgroup can still be proper.
A nontrivial subgroup contains an element other than the identity. A proper nontrivial subgroup is neither the identity-only subgroup nor the whole group.
The conjugate of h by g, in the convention here, is g⁻¹hg: change coordinates by g, apply h, then change back. Keeping all such elements in H characterizes the equal-left/right-coset property.

cards.title: Question 1
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). For \(a,b\in G\), define \(a\sim_R b\) if and only if \(ab^{-1}\in H\). Prove that \(\sim_R\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\).
cards.recallAnswer: Reflexivity: \(aa^{-1}=e\in H\). Symmetry: if \(ab^{-1}\in H\), its inverse \(ba^{-1}\) is in H. Transitivity: if \(ab^{-1}\) and \(bc^{-1}\) lie in H, closure gives \((ab^{-1})(bc^{-1})=ac^{-1}\in H\). These are precisely reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity, so the relation is an equivalence relation.

cards.q: Did you prove reflexivity and symmetry using the subgroup properties?

options.t: Only one property proved
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The identity and inverses belong to H.

cards.q: Did you prove transitivity in the correct multiplication order?

options.t: Closure cited without the correct product
Reordered noncommuting elements or no proof

cards.why: Cancellation is adjacent; commutativity is not assumed.

cards.label: Fraleigh §10 · Proof
cards.title: The three subgroup facts do all the work
cards.body: The first expression is in H by the identity property, the second by inverse closure, and the third by product closure. Therefore the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

cards.title: Remember
points: Right-coset relation here uses ab⁻¹, not a⁻¹b.
Inverse of a product reverses its factors.
Do not commute arbitrary group elements.

cards.title: Question 2
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Write all the left cosets of the subgroup \(3\mathbb Z\) in the additive group \(\mathbb Z\), and explain why they form a partition of \(\mathbb Z\).
cards.recallAnswer: The distinct cosets are \(3\mathbb Z\), \(1+3\mathbb Z\), and \(2+3\mathbb Z\). By division with remainder every integer has exactly one remainder 0, 1 or 2 modulo 3. Each coset is nonempty, every integer is in one of them, and no integer can have two different remainders. Thus these three cosets form a partition.

cards.q: Did you list the three distinct cosets?

options.t: \(3\mathbb Z,\ 1+3\mathbb Z,\ 2+3\mathbb Z\)
Two cosets or incomplete representative description
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Adding another multiple of 3 does not create a new coset.

cards.q: Did you establish nonemptiness, coverage and disjointness?

options.t: Unique remainder modulo 3 proves all three partition requirements
Only coverage or disjointness explained
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Listing sets alone is not a proof they partition the group.

cards.label: Fraleigh Example 10.3
cards.title: Classify integers by their remainders
cards.body: The dotted union means disjoint union. Negative integers also have a unique remainder in {0,1,2}, for example −1 belongs to 2+3Z.

cards.title: Remember
points: Additive cosets use addition, not products.
Representatives are 0, 1 and 2.
An infinite group can have a finite-index subgroup.

cards.title: Question 3
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Let \(G=\mathbb Z_{12}\) under addition modulo 12, and let \(H=\langle4\rangle\). Find all distinct cosets of H in G and write down the index \((G:H)\).
cards.recallAnswer: In Z₁₂, \(H=\{0,4,8\}\). Its distinct cosets are \(H\), \(1+H=\{1,5,9\}\), \(2+H=\{2,6,10\}\), and \(3+H=\{3,7,11\}\). These disjoint sets exhaust all twelve residues, so the index is 4, also \(|G|/|H|=12/3\).

cards.q: Did you find H and all four distinct cosets?

options.t: H correct but coset list incomplete
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The subgroup generated by 4 is formed by its multiples modulo 12.

cards.q: Did you give and justify the index?

options.t: Four cosets, or \(12/3=4\)
Correct number without justification
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The index counts cosets, not elements of H.

cards.title: Three elements in each of four cells
cards.body: Choose representatives 0,1,2,3. Adding 4 to a representative stays in its coset. Thus no new coset appears from representatives 4 through 11.

cards.title: Remember
points: Generate H first, then translate it.
List distinct cosets once each.
Group order equals subgroup order times index.

sheets.title: Q4 · Subgroup index
sheets.source: Fraleigh Definition 10.10 and §10 exercises; parity prerequisite

cards.title: Question 4
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Define the index of a subgroup H in a group G. Find (a) the index of \(A_n\) in \(S_n\) for \(n>1\), and (b) the index of \(5\mathbb Z\) in \((\mathbb Z,+)\).
cards.recallAnswer: The index (G:H) is the number of distinct left cosets of H in G; the same number counts right cosets. For n>1, S_n splits into even and odd permutations, so (S_n:A_n)=2. The cosets of 5Z in Z are r+5Z for r=0,1,2,3,4, giving index 5.

cards.q: Did you define index correctly?

options.t: Number of distinct left cosets, also equal to the number of right cosets
Only finite formula \(|G|/|H|\) without the general definition
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The second example has infinite G and H, so cardinal division is not an integer calculation here.

cards.q: Did you give both indices with reasons?

options.t: 2 from even/odd permutations; 5 from remainders modulo 5
One index justified
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: For n>1, multiplication by a transposition pairs even and odd permutations.

cards.title: Finite and infinite examples
cards.body: The first formula uses finite group sizes; the second is proved by counting five cosets, not by dividing two infinite cardinalities.

cards.title: Remember
points: Index counts cosets.
A_n consists of the even permutations.
For infinite groups use coset representatives rather than an informal infinity quotient.

cards.title: Question 5
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Let H be a subgroup of G and let a,b ∈ G. Prove that if \(aH=bH\), then \(Ha^{-1}=Hb^{-1}\).
cards.recallAnswer: Take elementwise inverses of the equal sets aH=bH. Since \((ah)^{-1}=h^{-1}a^{-1}\) and H is closed under inversion with H⁻¹=H, the inverse set of aH is Ha⁻¹. Likewise the inverse set of bH is Hb⁻¹. Equal sets have equal inverse sets, so Ha⁻¹=Hb⁻¹. No commutativity or normality is needed.

cards.q: Did you identify the inverse set correctly?

options.t: \((aH)^{-1}=H^{-1}a^{-1}=Ha^{-1}\), with order reversed
Inverse operation used but H⁻¹ = H unexplained
Kept the factors in the wrong order

cards.why: The inverse of ah is h⁻¹a⁻¹.

cards.q: Did you apply inversion to both equal sets and conclude?

options.t: Conclusion only
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: This is equality of sets, not a claim that a = b.

cards.label: Fraleigh Exercise 10.34 · Proof
cards.title: Inversion swaps the side
cards.body: For each subgroup element h, the inverse h⁻¹ again runs over all of H. This is why taking inverses turns a left coset into a right coset.

cards.title: Remember
points: Invert sets element by element.
Reverse product order when inverting.
No abelian hypothesis is required.

cards.title: Question 6
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Let H be a subgroup of G. Prove that for any a ∈ G the left coset aH has the same cardinality as H.
cards.recallAnswer: Define T:H→aH by T(h)=ah. It maps into aH by definition. If T(h₁)=T(h₂), left cancellation gives h₁=h₂, so T is injective. Every y in aH has the form ah for some h in H, so T is surjective. Thus T is a bijection and |aH|=|H|, for finite or infinite H.

cards.q: Did you define a suitable map and prove injectivity?

options.t: \(T(h)=ah\); cancellation gives a one-to-one map
Map correct but injectivity merely asserted
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Translation has inverse y↦a⁻¹y.

cards.q: Did you prove surjectivity and conclude equal cardinalities?

options.t: Every coset member is ah; hence T is onto and bijective
Conclusion without the onto argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The proof does not require finite groups.

cards.label: Fraleigh 10.6 · Proof
cards.title: Translate and translate back
cards.body: The displayed inverse is defined because y∈aH means a⁻¹y∈H. A two-sided inverse proves bijectivity and equal cardinalities directly.

cards.title: Remember
points: Equal size is proved by a bijection, not by assuming finiteness.
The inverse translation is multiplication by a⁻¹ on the left.
This fact is the counting engine of Lagrange's theorem.

cards.title: Question 7
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Prove that any group of prime order is cyclic and hence abelian.
cards.recallAnswer: Let |G|=p be prime and choose a≠e. The subgroup ⟨a⟩ has at least two elements and, by Lagrange, its order divides p. Hence |⟨a⟩|=p, so ⟨a⟩=G and G is cyclic. Every two elements are powers a^r and a^s, and a^r a^s=a^{r+s}=a^{s+r}=a^s a^r, so G is abelian.

cards.q: Did you use a nonidentity element and Lagrange to obtain a generator?

options.t: \(1<|\langle a\rangle|\mid p\), so \(\langle a\rangle=G\)
Prime-divisor argument incomplete
Chose only the identity or assumed cyclicity

cards.why: A prime has no divisor strictly between one and itself.

cards.q: Did you justify that cyclic implies abelian?

options.t: Products of powers commute because integer exponents add commutatively
Abelian asserted without justification
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The conclusion is about the operation in G, not just the integers.

cards.label: Fraleigh 10.8 · Proof
cards.title: Every nonidentity element generates
cards.body: Once every element is a power of a, the power rule proves commutativity. In fact every nonidentity element is a generator.

cards.title: Remember
points: Choose a ≠ e.
Apply Lagrange to the cyclic subgroup, not to an arbitrary subset.
Prime order implies cyclic, then abelian.

cards.title: Question 8
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Suppose G is a group of order 31. Can G have any subgroup other than {e} and G? Up to isomorphism, how many groups of order 31 exist? Justify your answer.
cards.recallAnswer: No other subgroup exists: Lagrange forces a subgroup order to divide the prime 31, so its order is 1 or 31. A prime-order group is cyclic. Every cyclic group of order 31 is isomorphic to Z₃₁ via [k]↦a^k for a generator a. Thus exactly one group of order 31 exists up to isomorphism.

cards.q: Did you exclude other subgroup orders by Lagrange?

options.t: Only divisors 1 and 31, giving {e} and G
Correct claim without a divisor argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A subgroup with 31 elements is the whole group.

cards.q: Did you justify the unique isomorphism class?

options.t: Prime order implies cyclic, so every such G is isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z_{31}\)
Cyclic stated without linking to uniqueness
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Unique up to isomorphism does not mean every realization has the same labels.

cards.title: One structure, different labels
cards.body: For a generator of order 31 this map is well-defined, bijective and preserves addition as multiplication. It realizes the claimed isomorphism.

cards.title: Remember
points: 31 is prime.
No proper nontrivial subgroup can have an allowed order.
All cyclic groups of one finite order are isomorphic.

cards.title: Question 9
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Show that if a finite group G with identity e has order n, then \(a^n=e\) for all a ∈ G. Hence calculate the remainder obtained when \(45^{72}\) is divided by 73.
cards.recallAnswer: Let d be the order of a. By Lagrange d divides n, say n=kd, so a^n=(a^d)^k=e. Since 73 is prime, the nonzero residue classes modulo 73 form a multiplicative group of order 72. The class of 45 lies in it, so 45^72≡1 (mod 73). The remainder is 1.

cards.q: Did you deduce the power identity from the element order?

options.t: \(d=o(a)\mid n\), so \(a^n=(a^d)^{n/d}=e\)
Correct claim without the order-divisibility argument
Assumed every element has order n

cards.why: Element order may be a proper divisor of the group order.

cards.q: Did you use the correct residue group and obtain the remainder?

options.t: Multiplicative nonzero residues modulo 73 have order 72; remainder 1
Remainder correct without a group justification
Used the additive group of order 73 for this exponent

cards.why: Exponentiation uses the multiplicative unit group.

cards.title: Choose the group that matches the operation
cards.body: 45 is nonzero modulo the prime 73, hence a unit. Applying Lagrange in the additive group Z₇₃ instead would be the wrong operation for this power calculation.

cards.title: Remember
points: The order of a divides n; it need not equal n.
The exponent identity comes from the cyclic subgroup.
For modular powers, use the multiplicative group of units.

cards.title: Question 10
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Does there exist a subgroup of a group of order 6 whose left cosets give a partition into (a) 6 cells, (b) 4 cells, (c) 12 cells? Give an example if possible, or explain why it is impossible.
cards.recallAnswer: For a group of order 6, the number of cosets is 6/|H|. (a) Six cells are possible with H={e}; its cosets are the six singleton sets. (b) Four cells would require |H|=6/4, not an integer, so impossible. (c) Twelve nonempty cells would require |H|=1/2, and even exceed the six available elements, so impossible.

cards.q: Did you supply the six-cell example?

options.t: H = {e} in any order-6 group, with singleton cosets
Yes without an example
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The identity subgroup has one element in each translate.

cards.q: Did you rule out both four and twelve cells?

options.t: Both counts give nonintegral subgroup orders under \(6=k|H|\)
Only one impossible count justified
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Allowed indices must divide six and cannot exceed six.

cards.title: Count equal-sized cells
cards.body: The theorem gives necessary index values. In part (a) the required example works for every group of order 6, regardless of whether it is abelian.

cards.title: Remember
points: Cosets are nonempty and all have size |H|.
Six singleton cells come from the identity subgroup.
A fractional subgroup size signals impossibility.

cards.title: Question 11
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Let \(G=\mathbb Z_{24}\) under addition modulo 24 and let \(H=\langle[3]\rangle\). List the elements of H, find all the cosets of H in G, and state the index of H in \(\mathbb Z_{24}\).
Did you list all elements of H?

options.t: Multiples of 3 identified with an incomplete list
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: All entries are residue classes modulo 24.

cards.q: Did you list the two other cosets and prove the list is complete?

options.t: 1+H and 2+H listed; three residue-mod-3 classes cover Z₂₄ disjointly
Two correct translates without completeness justification
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Each coset has eight elements and the union contains 24.

cards.q: Did you state the index?

options.t: Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Index counts the distinct cosets.

cards.title: Generate H first
cards.body: Repeated addition of 3 returns to zero after eight steps. The bracket notation denotes residue classes; representative numbers are used for readability.

cards.title: Translate by the remaining remainders
cards.body: Together with H, these sets contain every residue exactly once. Any other representative differs from 0,1 or 2 by a multiple of 3 and gives the same corresponding coset.

cards.title: Count the cells
cards.body: This check agrees with the explicit partition.

cards.title: Remember
points: Generate the subgroup before translating.
Arithmetic is modulo 24.
Eight elements per cell, three cells altogether.

cards.title: Question 12
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Let \(\sigma=(1,2,5,4)(2,3)\) be a permutation in \(S_5\). Express σ as a product of disjoint cycles, find the order of \(\langle\sigma\rangle\), and find the index of \(\langle\sigma\rangle\) in \(S_5\).
Did you compose the permutations consistently and obtain the disjoint cycle?

options.t: Right-to-left composition gives \((1\ 2\ 3\ 5\ 4)\); consistent opposite convention also accepted if stated
Correct mapping approach with one image error
Just concatenated the original cycle lengths

cards.why: The original cycles are not disjoint, so their lengths cannot yet be combined by an lcm.

cards.q: Did you find the subgroup order?

options.t: A 5-cycle has order 5, so \(|\langle\sigma\rangle|=5\)
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The cyclic subgroup order equals the generator's order.

cards.q: Did you compute and justify the index?

options.t: \((S_5:\langle\sigma\rangle)=5!/5=24\)
Correct index without the group-size argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: S₅ has 120 elements.

cards.label: Fraleigh §10 Exercise 15 · Work
cards.title: Apply the rightmost permutation first
cards.body: For instance, 3 first goes to 2 under (2 3), then to 5 under (1 2 5 4). These repeated images trace a single cycle containing all five symbols.

cards.title: Then use Lagrange's count
cards.body: The subgroup consists of the identity and σ,σ²,σ³,σ⁴. Under left-to-right composition the displayed cycle changes to (1 3 2 5 4), but its order and index remain 5 and 24.

cards.title: Remember
points: State the composition convention.
Find disjoint cycles before using their lengths.
The index is group order divided by cyclic subgroup order.

sheets.title: Q13 · Left and right in D4

cards.title: Question 13
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Find all the left cosets and all the right cosets of \(H=\langle\mu\rangle=\{\iota,\mu\}\) in \(D_4=\{\iota,\rho,\rho^2,\rho^3,\mu,\mu\rho,\mu\rho^2,\mu\rho^3\}\). Are the left cosets and right cosets of H the same? Justify.
Did you correctly list the four left cosets?

options.t: Two or three left cosets correct
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Use ρ^kμ = μρ^{−k}, with exponents modulo four.

cards.q: Did you correctly list the four right cosets?

options.t: Two or three right cosets correct
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Right multiplication by ρ^k gives {ρ^k,μρ^k} directly.

cards.q: Did you justify that the two partitions differ?

options.t: \(\rho H\ne H\rho\), with the different reflection partners exhibited
Said D₄ is nonabelian without checking these cosets
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Nonabelian groups can still have some subgroups whose left/right cosets agree, so use an explicit witness.

cards.label: Fraleigh Examples 10.5, 10.12
cards.title: The dihedral relation controls the side
cards.body: ρ is a quarter-turn rotation and μ a reflection. The formulas specify the multiplication convention needed to evaluate the cosets.

cards.title: Left cosets
cards.body: Each of the eight elements occurs exactly once. Thus the four sets are distinct and the list is complete.

cards.title: Right cosets
cards.body: Again the sets partition the eight elements. In particular the set containing ρ pairs it with a different reflection in the two lists, so the partitions do not agree.

cards.title: Remember
points: D₄ here has eight elements.
Left cosets require moving μ past a power of ρ.
Different left/right cosets still have the same size and the same number of cells.

sheets.title: Q14 · An index-two subgroup
sheets.source: Fraleigh Exercise 10.41 and coset partition properties

cards.title: Question 14
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Show that if H is a subgroup of index 2 in G, then every left coset of H is also a right coset of H. Hence prove that \(g^{-1}hg\in H\) for all g ∈ G and h ∈ H.
Did you handle g ∈ H and identify the unique outside left coset?

options.t: For \(g\in H\), \(gH=Hg=H\); otherwise \(gH=G\setminus H\)
Only the outside case explained
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: There are precisely two cells in the left-coset partition.

cards.q: Did you identify the outside right coset and conclude equality?

options.t: There are also two right cosets; \(Hg=G\setminus H\) outside H, hence \(gH=Hg\)
Equality asserted without the right-coset count
Assumed G finite unnecessarily and gave no general argument

cards.why: Inversion bijects left and right coset collections even for infinite G.

cards.q: Did you deduce the conjugation statement in the correct order?

options.t: hg ∈ Hg = gH, so hg = gh′ for h′ ∈ H and g⁻¹hg = h′
Correct conclusion with an incomplete membership argument
Reordered elements without justification

cards.why: No commutativity assumption is available.

cards.title: Only one other cell exists on either side
cards.tex: g\in H:\ gH=Hg=H;\qquad g\notin H:\ gH=G\setminus H=Hg
cards.body: The left index is two. Inversion sends aH to Ha⁻¹ and gives two right cosets too. Therefore each side's only outside cell is the complement of H, even if G is infinite.

cards.title: Convert coset membership into an equation
cards.body: For each h and g the coset equality supplies some h′ in H. Multiply the equation on the left by g⁻¹; no reordering is used.

cards.title: Remember
points: An index-two partition has H and its complement.
Left and right indices agree without finiteness.
Translate membership into a product equation before cancelling.

sheets.title: Q15 · Element order and its converse

cards.title: Question 15
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Define the order of an element in a group G. Show that in a finite group G the order of any element divides the order of G. Does every finite group contain an element of every order that divides the order of the group? Justify.
Did you define element order and relate it to a cyclic subgroup?

options.t: Least positive d with aᵈ = e, or infinite; \(o(a)=|\langle a\rangle|\)
Finite definition correct but relation to subgroup missing
Confused element order with group order

cards.why: In a finite group every element has finite order.

cards.q: Did you use Lagrange to prove divisibility?

options.t: Apply Lagrange to ⟨a⟩ ≤ G, so o(a) divides |G|
Divisibility asserted without the subgroup argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Lagrange applies to subgroups; the element statement is a corollary.

cards.q: Did you disprove the converse with a fully checked example?

options.t: \(\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2\) has order 4 but no element of order 4
Named a noncyclic group without checking its element orders
Claimed every divisor occurs as an element order

cards.why: Every nonidentity element of this group has order two.

cards.label: Fraleigh 10.9 · Proof
cards.title: Apply the counting theorem to the generated subgroup
cards.body: The elements e,a,…,a^{d−1} are distinct when d is the least positive return exponent; all higher powers reduce modulo d. Thus the generated subgroup has exactly d elements.

cards.title: A divisor need not be an element order
cards.body: All three nonidentity elements have order 2, so no element has order 4, even though 4 divides the group order. A finite cyclic group does realize every divisor, but arbitrary finite groups need not.

cards.title: Remember
points: Element order is a return exponent.
Its divisibility follows by applying Lagrange to ⟨a⟩.
Necessary divisibility does not guarantee an element with each divisor order.

sheets.title: Q16 · Proper subgroups of order pq

cards.title: Question 16
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Show that every proper subgroup of a group G, with \(o(G)=pq\) where p and q are prime numbers, is cyclic.
Did you use Lagrange and properness to list the possible subgroup orders?

options.t: Order divides pq but is not pq; possibilities are 1,p,q, with duplicates removed when p = q
Divisibility correct but trivial/equal-prime cases omitted
Assumed all proper subgroup orders equal p

cards.why: The primes are not stated to be distinct.

cards.q: Did you prove each allowed subgroup is cyclic?

options.t: Order one is trivial cyclic; prime order is cyclic by the prime-order theorem
Prime case correct but trivial case omitted
Claimed G itself must be cyclic

cards.why: The statement concerns proper subgroups, not the entire order-pq group.

cards.label: Fraleigh Exercise 10.36 · Proof
cards.title: List divisors, then exclude the whole group
cards.body: When p=q, the set reduces to {1,p}. A finite subgroup of the same order as G would equal G and is excluded by properness.

cards.title: Every remaining possibility is cyclic
cards.body: The identity-only subgroup is generated by e. Any subgroup of prime order is generated by every nonidentity element. Hence every proper subgroup in the question is cyclic.

cards.title: Remember
points: Do not assume p and q are distinct.
Include the trivial subgroup.
Nothing here claims the whole group of order pq is cyclic.

cards.title: Question 17
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Suppose \(K\le H\le G\) and both \((H:K)\) and \((G:H)\) are finite. Prove that \((G:K)\) is finite and \((G:K)=(G:H)(H:K)\).
Did you choose representative sets and show their products cover all K-cosets?

options.t: G = disjoint union a_iH, H = disjoint union b_jK; every g lies in some a_ib_jK
Representative construction correct but coverage incomplete
Used |G|/|H| despite possibly infinite groups

cards.why: Finite indices do not imply finite groups.

cards.q: Did you prove the rs cosets are distinct and conclude the index formula?

options.t: Equal product cosets force equal H-cosets, then equal K-cosets, so i and j coincide
Correct count asserted without distinctness proof
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A covering list may contain repetitions; distinctness must be checked.

cards.label: Fraleigh 10.11 · Proof 1
cards.title: Representatives inside representatives
cards.body: Each g∈G can be written a_ih with h∈H, then h=b_jk with k∈K. Thus g lies in one of the rs product cosets a_ib_jK.

cards.label: Proof 2
cards.title: Equal product cosets determine the first representative
cards.body: An element of either product coset belongs to both indicated H-cosets, because b_j and K lie in H. Intersecting cosets of H are equal; the chosen representatives were distinct.

cards.label: Proof 3
cards.title: Cancel and determine the second representative
cards.body: Left-multiply the equal sets by a_i⁻¹. The b_j representatives were chosen for distinct cosets of K in H.

cards.label: Conclusion
cards.title: Count the product cells
cards.body: There are exactly rs distinct K-cosets, a finite number. This proof works whether or not G and H have finite cardinality.

cards.title: Remember
points: Use coset representatives for possibly infinite groups.
Prove both coverage and no repetition.
The number of choices multiplies: r representatives outside, s inside.

cards.title: Question 18
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: (a) Show that a group with at least two elements but with no proper nontrivial subgroups must be finite and of prime order. (b) Using Lagrange's theorem, show that if n is odd, then an abelian group of order 2n contains at most one element of order 2.
Did you prove cyclicity and exclude an infinite cyclic group in part (a)?

options.t: Any a ≠ e generates G; if a has infinite order then ⟨a²⟩ is proper nontrivial
Cyclicity obtained but infinitude not ruled out
Assumed G finite at the start

cards.why: Lagrange cannot be applied to G before its finiteness is established.

cards.q: Did you exclude a composite finite order?

options.t: A cyclic group of composite order has a proper nontrivial subgroup generated by a suitable power
Composite case only asserted
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: If |G| = rs with r,s > 1, ⟨aʳ⟩ has order s.

cards.q: Did you construct the forbidden four-element subgroup in part (b)?

options.t: Distinct commuting order-two elements a,b give subgroup {e,a,b,ab} of order 4
Correct idea without closure or distinctness
Assumed ab has order four

cards.why: Commutativity gives (ab)²=e, and the four listed elements are distinct.

cards.q: Did you apply Lagrange and use oddness?

options.t: 4 would divide 2n, forcing n even, contradiction
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Only at most one is requested; existence is a different claim.

cards.label: Fraleigh Exercise 10.39 · Part (a)
cards.title: First show the group is cyclic
cards.body: Choose a ≠ e. Its generated subgroup is nontrivial and therefore cannot be proper, so G = ⟨a⟩. If a had infinite order, ⟨a²⟩ would be nontrivial and omit a, a contradiction.

cards.title: A composite cyclic order also gives a forbidden subgroup
cards.body: The group is finite by the preceding argument and has at least two elements. Composite order is impossible, so its order is prime.

cards.label: Fraleigh Exercise 10.38 · Part (b)
cards.title: Two different involutions would generate four elements
cards.body: If a and b are distinct and nonidentity, ab is neither e nor a nor b, by cancellation. Commutativity lets every product reduce to one of these four elements; each is its own inverse.

cards.title: Lagrange forbids that subgroup
cards.body: This contradicts odd n. Therefore two distinct elements of order two cannot exist, proving the requested at-most-one statement.

cards.title: Remember
points: Part (a) must rule out infinite cyclic groups before using finite-order arguments.
For composite cyclic order, a proper power generates a proper nontrivial subgroup.
Part (b) uses abelianity to make a four-element subgroup.
The contradiction is 4 dividing twice an odd integer.

sections.title: Section C · 10 marks each · best one

sheets.title: Q19 · Coset classes and block table

cards.title: Question 19
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: (a) Let H be a subgroup of G. Define \(a\sim_L b\) iff \(a^{-1}b\in H\). Prove that this is an equivalence relation and show that the cell containing a is \(aH=\{ah:h\in H\}\). (b) Find the partition of \(\mathbb Z_6\), under addition modulo 6, into cosets of \(H=\{0,3\}\). Construct the group table for \(\mathbb Z_6\) with elements arranged in the order of these cosets and show that the coset blocks form a group isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z_3\).
Did you prove all three equivalence properties?

options.t: Identity, inverse and product arguments for \(a^{-1}b\in H\), with correct multiplication order
Only two properties fully proved
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: For transitivity multiply a⁻¹b by b⁻¹c.

cards.q: Did you identify the class containing a as aH in both directions?

options.t: \(a^{-1}b\in H\iff b=ah\) for some h ∈ H
Only one inclusion
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Membership equivalence proves equality of the two sets.

cards.q: Did you list the three cosets and construct the full reordered table?

options.t: {0,3},{1,4},{2,5}, and correct 6×6 addition table in order 0,3,1,4,2,5
Cosets right but table incomplete or with isolated errors
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The table entries are sums modulo six, grouped into 2×2 blocks.

cards.q: Did you show the block operation is well-defined and isomorphic to Z3?

options.t: Coset addition independent of representatives; block table and bijection C_i↦[i]₃ preserve addition
Correct block table or map without well-definedness
Claimed arbitrary cosets always form a group

cards.why: Here the additive group is abelian, so adding subgroup elements does not change the resulting coset.

cards.label: Fraleigh 10.1 · Part (a)
cards.title: Equivalence from the subgroup axioms
cards.body: The identity is in H, inverses of H-elements stay in H, and products of H-elements stay in H. Thus the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

cards.title: The equivalence cell is exactly a left coset
cards.body: If a⁻¹b=h∈H then b=ah. Conversely b=ah gives a⁻¹b=h∈H. Both inclusions are explicit.

cards.label: Fraleigh Example 10.13 · Part (b)
cards.title: The three cells in Z6
cards.body: They are the distinct translates of H, cover all six residues, and are pairwise disjoint.

cards.label: Fraleigh Table 10.14
cards.title: The full reordered addition table
cards.body: Row and column labels are 0,3,1,4,2,5. Every entry is its row label plus its column label modulo 6. Each 2×2 block contains elements from just one coset.

cards.title: Representative choices do not affect the block
cards.body: Replacing a or b by another representative of its coset changes the sum only by a member of H. Therefore C_i+C_j is a well-defined coset, namely C_{i+j mod 3}.

cards.label: Fraleigh Table 10.15
cards.title: The block table
cards.body: C₀ is the identity, C₁ and C₂ are inverses, and associativity is inherited from addition of residues. This is the addition pattern of Z₃.

cards.title: An explicit isomorphism
cards.body: The map is bijective and preserves the operation. Thus the coset-block group is isomorphic to Z₃. This construction is justified here, rather than assumed for arbitrary subgroups.

cards.title: Remember
points: The left-coset equivalence uses a⁻¹b.
Identify the class by proving membership in both directions.
Reorder both rows and columns of the actual Z₆ table.
Prove the block operation is independent of representatives before claiming a group.
The three blocks add exactly like residues modulo three.

cards.title: Question 20
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: (a) Let H be a subgroup of a finite group G. State and prove Lagrange's theorem, showing that the order of H divides the order of G. (b) Use Lagrange's theorem to prove Euler's theorem: if a,n ∈ Z with n > 0 and gcd(a,n)=1, then \(a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n\). Hence deduce Fermat's little theorem.
Did you state Lagrange and justify the coset partition?

options.t: H ≤ finite G; left cosets partition G into finitely many cells
Statement correct but partition not justified
Claimed a converse or omitted finiteness

cards.why: Cosets are equivalence classes, so disjointness and coverage are established.

cards.q: Did you prove equal coset size and the divisibility count?

options.t: h↦ah bijects H to aH; \(|G|=(G:H)|H|\)
Count given without proving equal coset cardinality
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: An equally sized partition is the entire counting proof.

cards.q: Did you apply Lagrange to the correct unit group to prove Euler?

options.t: U(n) has φ(n) elements; gcd(a,n)=1 puts [a] in it; element order divides φ(n), giving Euler; n = 1 handled
Correct power argument without identifying the group or its size
Used the additive residue group for powers

cards.why: The operation is multiplication modulo n.

cards.q: Did you deduce Fermat with both forms and the divisibility case?

options.t: For prime p, a^{p−1} ≡ 1 if p∤a, and a^p ≡ a for every integer a
Only the coprime form, without the all-integer conclusion
Claimed a^{p−1} ≡ 1 even when p divides a

cards.why: If p divides a, the a^p ≡ a form holds because both sides are zero modulo p.

cards.label: Fraleigh 10.7 · Statement
cards.title: A finite group is tiled by equal-sized cosets
cards.body: If H is a subgroup of finite G, then |H| divides |G|. The cosets partition G, and multiplication h↦ah is a bijection from H to each coset. Count their sizes to finish.

cards.title: The count behind Lagrange
cards.legend: Let n = |G|, m = |H| and r = (G:H). Cosets are disjoint and exhaust G; each has m elements by the translation bijection.

steps.note: Count the elements of the coset partition.
Translation h↦a_ih bijects H onto each cell.

ask.q: Why do all cells have m elements?
options: Multiplication by a representative is a bijection
Every subset has the same size
ask.why: The inverse translation is multiplication by a_i⁻¹.

ask.q: Why can the cell sizes be added without overcounting?
ask.why: Distinct cosets are disjoint and their union is G.

ask.q: What makes m a divisor of n?
ask.why: n is m times the integer number of cosets.

steps.note: This also gives the finite index formula.

ask.q: Which hypothesis made this a finite integer count?
ask.why: Lagrange's ordinary order-divisibility statement is for finite groups.

cards.label: Part (b) · Fraleigh §24
cards.title: Use the multiplicative group of units
cards.body: For n ≥ 2 these classes form a group under multiplication: products remain invertible, [1] is identity, and every class has an inverse by Bézout's identity. The totient counts these classes by definition.

cards.title: Euler follows from the element-order corollary
cards.body: The coprimality hypothesis puts [a] in U(n). The displayed group identity is exactly a^{φ(n)} ≡ 1 modulo n. For n = 1 the congruence is automatic, so that case requires no separate unit-group convention.

cards.title: Specialize to a prime modulus
cards.body: Every nonzero residue modulo the prime p is a unit, giving p−1 such classes. This is Fermat's little theorem in its coprime form.

cards.title: The all-integer form of Fermat
cards.body: If p∤a, multiply the coprime form by a. If p|a, both a and a^p are zero modulo p. Do not assert the exponent-(p−1) form when a is divisible by p.

cards.title: Remember
points: Lagrange counts cosets of an actual subgroup.
Euler uses the multiplicative unit group, whose order is φ(n).
Coprimality is membership in that group.
For prime p, φ(p)=p−1.
Fermat's a^p ≡ a form includes multiples of p; the a^{p−1} ≡ 1 form does not.
